sources.title: Walker: Reclaiming Māori education (2016)
sources.citation: Ranginui Walker, “Reclaiming Māori education,” in Jessica Hutchings and Jenny Lee-Morgan, eds., Decolonisation in Aotearoa: Education, Research and Practice (NZCER Press, 2016), 19–38.

verification.note: Publisher’s chapter PDF freshly checked: selected pp. 19–20, 23–24, 25–29 and conclusion/reference pp. 36–38 read; p. 24 visually collated. Explicit Foucault use concerns curricular exclusion and knowledge hierarchy; p. 37 prints Knowledge/Power. This is not a whole-chapter reading or a claim to have read Foucault’s original. Freire appears on p. 20 but has no existing graph endpoint; no new biography requested. The 2016 chapter is distinct from the 1990 book and its revised 2004 edition.

sources.title: Adds and colleagues: Walker’s Gramsci use in media analysis (2005)
sources.citation: Peter Adds, Maia Bennett, Meegan Hall, Bernard Kernot, Marie Russell and Tai Walker, The Portrayal of Māori and Te Ao Māori in Broadcasting: The Foreshore and Seabed Issue (Broadcasting Standards Authority, 2005), 47–48, §2.2.3.

verification.note: Primary report’s title, six-person research-team credit, copyright 2005, selected literature-review pp. 46–48 and bibliography p. 140 entry for Walker 2002 freshly read; p. 47 visually collated. Report explicitly says Ranginui Walker cites Gramsci on domination and intellectual/moral leadership in Māori news is bad news, then explains the one-sided media discourse. Walker’s 2002 chapter, its complete evidence, and Gramsci’s original passage/edition remain unread. Tai Walker, report coauthor, is not Ranginui Walker. No whole-report reading claimed.

sources.title: Byrnes and Coleborne: Fanon and Walker’s counter-history (2011)
sources.citation: Giselle Byrnes and Catharine Coleborne, “Editorial Introduction: The Utility and Futility of ‘The Nation’ in Histories of Aotearoa New Zealand,” New Zealand Journal of History 45.1 (2011), 1–14, esp. 8 and note 48,13–14.

verification.note: Freshly read selected historiographical discussion pp. 7–8 and note 48 across pp. 13–14; p. 8 and both note pages visually collated in institutional PDF. Joint authors explicitly identify Walker’s Fanon inspiration and colonial-disavowal/resistance interpretation, citing the revised 2004 book and Fanon’s 1965/1968 London editions. These originals remain unread. This is qualified named-reader evidence, not a newly verified direct quotation from Walker or an inference from shared postcolonial vocabulary.

sources.title: Smith: Walker as an example of scholarly responsibility (2022)
sources.citation: Linda Tuhiwai Smith, in conversation with Te Rina Warren, “A Conversation with Professor Linda Tuhiwai Smith,” Te Tiriti-based Futures and Anti-racism,27 March 2022, transcript 8–9.

verification.note: Organizer-hosted primary transcript selected pp. 1, 8–9 and 15 freshly read; p. 9 visually collated. Speaker labels assign the Walker example to Professor Tuhiwai Smith. Date 27 March appears on p. 1; event year 2022 appears on p. 15 and interviewer’s institutional CV independently lists 27 Mar 2022. PDF search metadata incorrectly says 30 July 2001; the document and event evidence control. Smith invokes Walker’s public defense in her own answer about community responsibility; no personal mentoring claim or audiovisual viewing. Corroborating date metadata: https://www.massey.ac.nz/massey/expertise/profile.cfm?stref=952050 .
